client: I've been really struggling since I got laid off last month — the company downsized and I was one of the people let go. Rent is due next week and I honestly don't know how I'm going to cover it, and that thought is just constantly running through my head. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change the fact that I need money, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely heavy — the uncertainty about rent, the job loss, all of it swirling around at once, and I completely understand the part of you that wonders what talking can even do when the practical pressure is so real. You're right that our conversation won't pay the rent, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But sometimes when a worry is running on a loop like that, it can help to look at what that loop is telling you about yourself and your options — what does that voice in your head say is going to happen if you can't cover rent next week?

client: The voice basically tells me I'm going to lose my apartment, end up with nowhere to go, and that it's proof I can't handle my own life. Like, it jumps straight from "rent is due" to "you're a complete failure who's going to be on the street," and I know that sounds extreme when I say it out loud. But in my head at 2am it feels completely logical and inevitable.
therapist: It's actually a really important moment that you noticed it sounds extreme when you say it out loud — that gap between the 2am feeling and the daylight version of it is worth paying attention to. That mental jump from "rent is due" to "I'm a complete failure headed for the street" is what we'd call a thinking trap, where your mind skips over all the steps in between and lands straight on the worst possible outcome. What are some of those steps in between that your mind is glossing over — things you could actually do, or people or resources that exist between "rent is due" and "I'm on the street"?

client: I guess there are some things — like I could talk to my landlord and ask for a few extra days, or I could look into whether I qualify for any kind of emergency assistance. I also have a couple of friends I could theoretically ask for help, but that one feels really hard because I don't want them to see me as someone who can't manage their own life. It's like even naming these options makes me feel embarrassed, which is weird because I know I'd help any of them without judging them for it.
therapist: You just did something really significant — you went from "there's nothing I can do" to naming three concrete options, and that's your own mind problem-solving even under stress. And that last thing you said is so worth sitting with: you'd help a friend in this situation without a second thought or any judgment, yet you're holding yourself to a completely different standard. What do you think it says about you as a person that your first instinct when imagining a friend in need is generosity — and is there any reason they wouldn't extend that same feeling back to you?

client: I mean, logically I know my friends care about me and probably wouldn't judge me the way I'm judging myself. But there's this part of me that feels like the layoff somehow changed things, like it's exposed something about me that makes me less worthy of that kind of support. I hear what you're saying about the double standard, and it makes sense in theory, but actually picking up the phone and asking someone for help still feels almost impossible.
therapist: There's something really painful in what you just described — this sense that the layoff didn't just change your circumstances, but somehow changed your *worth*, like it revealed a flaw that was always there. That belief — "I am less deserving of support because of something that happened *to* me" — is worth gently challenging, because a company's decision about headcount isn't actually evidence about your value as a person or a friend. When you imagine picking up the phone and calling one of those friends, what specifically do you picture them thinking or saying — and how much of that is based on who they've actually shown themselves to be versus what this painful moment is telling you they'll think?

client: When I actually think about my friend Jamie specifically, she's never once made me feel judged for struggling — she's the kind of person who checks in without being asked. But I'm still picturing this scenario where I call her and she's kind on the surface but secretly thinks less of me, and I realize that's probably more about the story I'm telling myself than anything she's actually done. I guess what scares me is that asking for help makes the whole situation more real, like saying it out loud to someone who knows me means I can't pretend I have it together anymore.
therapist: You just showed real clarity there — recognizing that the story about Jamie is yours, not hers, and that her actual track record tells a completely different story. And what you said about asking for help making it "more real" is so honest and important — there's something that feels protective about keeping up the appearance of having it together, even when it costs you the support you actually need. I'm curious: is it possible that letting it be real with someone who loves you might feel less like losing control, and more like finally setting down something you've been carrying alone?

client: That framing actually hits differently — "setting something down" instead of losing control. I've been so focused on what asking for help would cost me that I haven't really let myself think about what it might feel like to not be alone with this for even one conversation. But I'm still scared that once I say it out loud to Jamie, I won't be able to hold it together emotionally, and I don't want to fall apart on her.
therapist: It's really moving to hear that shift in you — from bracing for loss to glimpsing the relief that might be on the other side. And I want to gently offer this: "falling apart" in front of someone who cares about you isn't a failure of composure, it's actually what allows real connection to happen, and Jamie checking in on you without being asked suggests she's someone who can hold that with you. What if the version of you that cries or struggles on that call is exactly the version of you that Jamie would feel trusted and honored to show up for?

client: That's a really different way of looking at it, and part of me wants to believe it's true. But I also have this deeply ingrained thing where showing emotion feels like burdening someone, like I'm making my problem their problem, and I've spent so long trying not to be "too much" for people. I don't know how to just switch that off even if I intellectually understand what you're saying.
therapist: That belief — "my emotions are a burden, I am too much" — sounds like it's been with you for a long time, and it makes so much sense that it doesn't just dissolve because you intellectually see through it. These deeply held beliefs about ourselves usually formed for a reason, often as a way of staying safe or keeping connection with people who maybe couldn't handle our full selves at some point. I'm curious — when you trace that feeling of being "too much" back, where do you think it first came from, and is Jamie actually someone from that same story, or is she someone who's shown you a different kind of relationship is possible?

client: Honestly, I think it goes back to my mom — she had her own struggles and I learned pretty early that bringing my problems to her usually made things harder, so I just stopped. Jamie is genuinely nothing like that, she's actually proven over and over that she can handle the real version of me, but knowing that intellectually and feeling safe enough to act on it are two completely different things. It's like my nervous system hasn't gotten the memo that not every relationship works the same way.
therapist: What you just described is such an important insight — your nervous system learned a very real lesson early on, that vulnerability led to more pain rather than relief, and it's been trying to protect you ever since. The beautiful and hopeful thing is that you can already see the distinction clearly: Jamie isn't your mom, and that pattern you learned, as understandable as it is, is running on old data. Change at that deeper felt level usually happens not through more convincing yourself intellectually, but through small moments of risk that give your nervous system new experiences to learn from — so I'm wondering, what might it look like to take just one tiny step with Jamie, something small enough to feel manageable, that could start giving that part of you some new evidence?

client: Maybe I could text her instead of calling — something like "hey, I'm going through a rough patch, can we talk soon?" without having to be fully vulnerable in real time. That feels slightly less terrifying because I'd have a second to think before I send it, and I wouldn't have to hear her reaction immediately. But I'm already worrying that I'll type it out and then just stare at it for an hour without hitting send.
therapist: That text idea is genuinely a perfect first step — it's honest, it's low-pressure, and it still opens the door, which takes real courage even if it doesn't feel that way. The "staring at it without hitting send" worry is worth naming though, because that hesitation is just the old protective pattern doing its job one last time before you do something new. What if we thought about one small thing you could put in place right now — like a specific time today you'd write the text — that makes it a little harder for that hesitation to win?

client: I could say I'll do it at 7pm tonight, after dinner when I'm not rushing around, but I'm a little skeptical of my own commitment because I've made deals with myself before and then found a reason to back out. I think what might actually help is telling you right now what I'm going to say in the text, so it feels more real and less like something I can quietly abandon later. Does that make sense, or does it sound like I'm just stalling?
therapist: That doesn't sound like stalling at all — it sounds like you know yourself really well, and you're using that self-knowledge to set yourself up for success rather than quietly letting yourself off the hook. Saying it out loud here makes it more concrete and real, and there's something meaningful about having witnessed it together. So tell me — what does the text to Jamie say?
